Through soil erodibility appraisals, and evaluations of compaction and displacement hazards, areas that could suffer irreversible damage of long duration from machines can be identified. By identifying areas susceptible to such deterioration, damage could be minimized by prohibiting this type of use. Controlled use on areas with minimum susceptibility would result in a reduction of soil movement, compaction, and displacement.
ORV use may affect the physical, chemical, biological, and aesthetic qualities of water. Indiscriminate use of machines in some areas may rut slopes, breakdown stream banks or loosen soil in or adjacent to streams so that erosion and siltation can occur. Use of machines in stream beds can affect the spawning, migrating, and feeding habits of fish and other aquatic life. Use of over-snow vehicles for fishing purposes may result in some water pollution from litter and waste left on the ice. Vehicles can affect water quality by adding oils, greases, scum, and other matter. Water quality may be maintained or only slightly diminished where the use of ORV in and adjacent to water courses is controlled.
There is an impact on air from ORV use. The impact may be dust created by vehicles traveling on dusty trails or across areas that are sparsely vegetated with loose soils. Emissions from internal combustion engines also adversely affect air quality. These impacts are likely to increase with the number of vehicles involved, the type of soil on which they are used, the type of ORV, and the speed of the vehicle.
B) Biologic Impacts:
Plants, animals, fish, and other living things are prevalent on our public lands. Indiscriminate use of ORV, particularly off of designated trails and in fragile or sensitive areas, can have severe irreversible and irretrievable harmful effects on the biota.
Many plant communities are vulnerable to damage by ORV traffic. Communities characterized by slow growth, sparse or fragile vegetation, such as desert or tundra, or occurring on sites with harsh growing conditions, can suffer long-term damage. Communities of rare plant species may be damaged.
Areas recently revegetated to grass or shrub species as well as tree plantations and areas naturally recovering from earlier ecological disturbance are particularly susceptible. The control of vehicular traffic on these sites will help protect them and maintain the desirable diversity and stability of their ecosystems. Control will also minimize damage to forage resources for livestock and wildlife.
